“Wake me in the morning,” he said, already quieter. “Don’t let me sleep all day.” A pause. “Unless you want to.”

She kissed his temple. “Go to sleep.”

And he did. Not because his body had made him. He slept because he was warm, and somebody was holding his hand, and the room was quiet, and for once he did not feel that he had to stay awake to keep himself alive.

His mug stood on the bench with its name turned to the wall. She noticed it after a while, and reached over with her free hand, and turned it round to face the room.

chapters.title: What He Does for Work
chapters.desc: Mouse finds the missing Belgian in a newspaper. Serafina lays out everything she knows on the workbench, and he doesn’t tell her she’s wrong.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.”
chapters.content:
Mouse came in at sixteen minutes past ten on the second Saturday in January with two coffees, a paper bag of pastries, and the face of a woman who had found something she very much wished she hadn’t.

Serafina looked up from the gearbox on the bench. “That’s a terrible face.”

“Good morning to you too.” Mouse put the coffees down. She didn’t take her coat off. “Remember the Belgian?”

Serafina’s hand stopped. There were a great many Belgians in the world. Only one had been walked out of a government reception by a man who wasn’t a guard and put into the back of a car that sat too low on its springs.

“Marchal.”

“I found him.” Mouse took a folded printout out of her bag. “Not where. In a newspaper.”

It was a Brussels paper, in French. A photograph of a tall fair man in a grey suit, smiling at what looked like a wedding: Lucien Marchal (46). Under it, smaller, a woman on a doorstep in Antwerp with her hand over her mouth, and two teenage boys behind her. A family appeal, a week old. He had been last seen at a reception on Battery Hill in October. The police here said he had left the city. The police there said he had never arrived.

“His ticket home was used on the twenty-third,” said Mouse, very flat. “He wasn’t on the plane.”

Serafina read it twice. She remembered the fair man’s face going the colour of paper. She remembered him walking anyway, with a hand at his elbow, not gripping.

Mouse leaned on the bench. “There’s something else. I swept the place last night. After you told me about the brakes, and the knocks at two in the morning, I thought I’d look.” She put a small thing down on the steel between them. A lens on a sliver of circuit board, no bigger than a fingernail, with a hair of wire trailing off it. “It was in the roof. Over the lift. Pointing at the bench. Pointing at you.”

Serafina looked at it for a long time. Then she picked up her coffee, and found that her hand wasn’t steady, and put it down again.

“Have you asked him?” said Mouse.

The answer was no. She had thought about it every night since October. But now there was a mug with his name on the bottom. His coffee in her cupboard. His spare jacket on the hook behind the office door. And a newspaper from Brussels.

“I’ll ask him,” she said. “When he comes.”

“He always comes,” she added, and it sounded less like confidence than like something she had got used to leaning on. Mouse pushed one of the coffees closer and said, “Drink it before it goes cold,” and went to sit behind her screens without putting her headphones on, which she never did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu came in at noon with a crate of oil, put it down very gently, and came and leaned on the bench next to her, not looking at what she’d laid out on it. Looking at his own hands.

“You going to tell him to go?”

“I don’t know.”

“Two stretches, me. You know that. You never asked what for. Week I got out, you gave me a key. Said the kettle’s there, the toilet’s out the back, don’t touch Gilded’s gearbox.” He rubbed his thumb over an old scar on his knuckle. “Nobody else gave me a key.”

“That’s different. You didn’t take anyone’s dad, Wu.”

Big Wu was quiet for a while. “No,” he said. “I didn’t.” He pushed off the bench. “I’m only saying. You’re the one with the keys. You decide who gets one. Always have.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Haozhen came at eight forty-two. She heard the grey car in the alley, the brakes biting clean at the corner, her brakes, and then the side door. He came in, and stopped.

There was no coffee waiting for him. She had laid it all out on the bench under the work lamp the way she laid out the symptoms of a car nobody else could fix, in a row, until they stopped being separate things and turned into one. A photograph of the grey estate. The Autumn Reception guest list. A strip of black cotton, frayed at one end, which she had found caught in the runner of his back seat in December and kept without knowing why. A photograph of a dark van, taken by a delivery camera in the lane on the old ring road. The photocopy from Auntie Chu: Qin H. East service. 19:02. The camera from the roof. And in the middle, the woman on the doorstep in Antwerp.

He took his gloves off, slowly. “What’s all this?”

“Your hobbies.”

He looked at her. She didn’t smile.

His face didn’t change when he saw the newspaper. That was the first thing she noticed. No surprise. No irritation. He read the headline.

“His family?”

“Antwerp. A wife and two sons. Nobody’s heard from him since October.”

He put his gloves down beside the paper. “That’s unfortunate.”

She laughed, once, in disbelief. “Unfortunate?”

“Serafina—“

“Don’t.” She held up the photograph of the van between two fingers. “This is what he went into. Registered to a company with a director who died six years ago. Same trick as your car. This is your car. You changed the plates after the reception, but the scrape on the back left corner is the same scrape.” She put it down. “I found the brakes. I found the company. I found the sign-in sheet. I found your name. I watched you take a man out of a building and put him in a car. And now his children are in the newspaper.” She looked at him. “Tell me I’ve got it wrong.”

He didn’t. The silence weighed more than any denial.

“Who are you?”

He looked tired. He looked like a man who had come round to spend the evening with his girlfriend. “I move people,” he said at last.

Her fingers closed on the edge of the bench. “Move them where?”

“Where they’re supposed to go.”

“Police? Military? The government?”

He neither confirmed nor denied any of it.

“Was Marchal a criminal?”

“I can’t tell you that.”

“Was he alive when you handed him over?”

“Yes.” It came at once. “He was conscious. He was breathing. He could walk, though he’d rather not have. Two men in a van, under a broken streetlight on the old ring road. I don’t know what happened after. I’m not told. Mostly I’m not told.”

“And you don’t ask?”

“I was eighteen. They’d told me since I was sixteen that asking was somebody else’s job.” He looked at the paper. “Once you’ve done it without asking, it’s very hard to start.”

“His wife is looking for him. His sons.”

His jaw moved, very slightly. “I know.”

“Then how do you sleep?”

For the first time, he looked away. Not for long. Long enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had imagined this a dozen ways. In one he laughed and told her she’d misunderstood. In another he explained that Marchal was a danger to a great many people and there were reasons she couldn’t see. She hadn’t imagined this: him standing in her garage looking at a photograph of a man’s family as if it were a piece of information he had already accounted for.

She came round the end of the bench, so there was more space between them, and made herself ask it. “Do you kill people?”

He didn’t move. The question seemed to take something out of the air.

“Sometimes,” he said.

She felt the word land before she understood it. She looked at his hands. She knew those hands. She knew them on a steering wheel, at a quarter to three. She knew how they passed her a socket before she asked for it, and how carefully they had wiped oil off the corner of her mouth. She had never once let herself think about what else they had done.

“Was Marchal one of them?”

“No.”

“Would you have?”

He considered it, which was the worst thing he could have done. “If I’d been told to.”

She took a step back. “That’s a horrible thing to say.”

“I know.”

“You’re telling me the parts of the truth you can afford.”

He held her eyes. “I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.”

“I’d rather you were someone else,” she said, and it was out before she could stop it, and she saw it reach him. He didn’t flinch. He took it, and that was how she knew it had gone in. “I’m sorry,” she said.

“Don’t be.”

“Have you done it since you met me? Taken someone? And then come here and drunk coffee out of that mug?”

A long pause. “Yes.”

“When?”

“The Tuesday before Christmas.”

She shut her eyes. The Tuesday before Christmas he had come in after midnight and sat on the sofa while she fought a seized bolt, and reached over without a word and loosened it for her, and later she had fallen asleep against his shoulder, and he had held her till it was light. She had thought it was an ordinary night. Perhaps, to him, it had been. Perhaps that was what frightened her most.

She picked the camera off the bench and held it up between them. “And this? Is this why there was a camera in my roof pointing at my bench?”

His face tightened. “I had the footage taken down.”

“You had the camera put up.”

“Yes.”

“You watched me.”

“I watched the building.”

“No, Haozhen. Don’t make it sound different from what it was.”

Something moved under his face then. Not the composure. Something beneath it. “I don’t want you in this.”

“I’m already in it.”

“You don’t get to keep me beside you when you want me and keep half of yourself locked in a room I’m not allowed into.”

“Serafina—“

“Do you know the number? How many?”

He went very still. “Yes. Every one. Names. Dates. Where. What they were wearing. I don’t let myself forget them.”

“Then I don’t want it,” she said. “Not tonight. Not the names, not the stories. Not a number you’d give me and expect me to know what to do with.”

“If you ever want it, ask me, and I’ll tell you all of it. Not standing up, with that photograph on your bench.”

“Then leave,” she said.

He looked at her for a long moment. “Do you want me to leave?”

“Yes.” He didn’t move. She swallowed. “Yes. I do.”

He nodded once, as if she had told him the time. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He put his coat on without hurrying. He didn’t argue, and that made her angrier than anything else he could have done. At the door he stopped with his hand on the frame and his back to her.

“If you tell anyone about this—“

She went cold all over. “Then what?”

He turned his head. “Then nothing. I’d make sure nobody touched you for it. That’s all I was going to say.” His knuckles had gone white on the frame. It was the only part of him that moved. “Lock this door after me. And the shutter. You leave the shutter up at night. You shouldn’t.”

Then he came back across the garage. Not fast. Past the bench and the row of evidence and the camera. He stopped in front of her, close enough that she could feel the cold of the alley still on his coat, and his hands stayed at his sides where she could see them, the way they had on the first night.

“May I?”

She should have said no. She stood very still. His fingers came to her jaw, gently enough to make her throat ache, and he kissed her once. Quiet, and restrained, and unbearably familiar, as if he were learning her face well enough to keep it.

She kissed him back. Furious with him, with herself, with a doorstep in Antwerp. She took his coat in both fists and pulled him in and kissed him as though she could make him answer for every word he’d refused to say, and her face was wet, and she didn’t know when that had started. She was the one who stopped. She put her hand flat on his chest and pushed. Not hard. He went back one step and no further.

“Don’t do that,” she said.

“I’m sorry.”

“Go.”

He went. The side door closed. A moment later she heard the grey car start in the alley, and the brakes at the corner, clean, and then nothing.

His mug was on the shelf, name to the wall. She took it down. She put it upside down on the bench, and walked away from it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past eleven she drove the loop alone. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. No music. Her body had learned it his way: no hard braking, the engine murmuring in third. On the coast road, at the bend where his head always slid onto her shoulder, she dropped her right shoulder a fraction to catch it. There was nobody there.

She put her foot down then. For a few seconds there was nothing but speed, and then she lifted, and turned into the lay-by above the harbour, and killed the engine. The silence came in like water.

A wife in Antwerp. Two boys. A man who had been alive when he was handed over. Sometimes.

She put her forehead on the wheel. “Fuck,” she said, and her voice sounded very small in the car.

Then she cried. Not the quiet kind she could wipe off. Her shoulders shook and her nose ran and she made an ugly helpless noise. She thought of him asleep in the passenger seat. Two hours and eleven minutes. She thought of him saying Sometimes. She hit the wheel with the heel of her hand. “Goddamn you,” she said, and it came apart in the middle.

She got out into the cold and let the sound out, a raw furious howl that put a bird up out of the dark somewhere below, and bent over with her hands on her knees and cried until her throat hurt. Nobody came.

When she got back in, she looked at the empty passenger seat for a long time. For the first time since December she didn’t want to drive anybody home. She drove herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was parked on the old service road below the lay-by with his lights off. He had followed her from the end of her street, two cars back. He knew where she would go.

He watched her car rock a little on its springs when she hit the wheel. He heard her, when she got out. The sound came down the hill and across the road, and he heard her voice break, and he sat with his hands on his own wheel and did nothing. She had told him to go. He had gone. He only made sure nobody else stopped in that lay-by. A van slowed, once. He flashed his lights at it, and it thought better of it.

His breathing was wrong. Too fast. His phone lit up on the passenger seat. Transfer confirmation pending. Call when available. He looked at it, and turned the phone off. Then he turned it back on, typed Are you under her name, deleted it, and put the phone face down on the empty seat.

He followed her home, and watched her go up the iron stairs to the flat above the garage. He stood under the overhang of the print works at the end of the alley. He knew which window was hers. At a quarter past two her light went out. At four it began to rain. At half past five the first delivery van came through and its headlights slid over the wet stones. He did not sleep. He hadn’t expected to.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came down the iron stairs at twelve minutes past six with her hair up and her face washed in cold water until the red had nearly gone, and the first thing she saw was the grey estate at the end of the alley. The second was him, beside it, his coat dark with rain, his hands in his pockets.

She stopped on the bottom step.

“You followed me. To the harbour.”

“Yes.”

“Did you watch me?”

“I stayed across the road.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

A pause. “Yes.”

“I told you to leave, and you don’t get to decide you can stand outside my house all night instead.”

“Then what were you doing here?”

“Making sure nobody followed you.”

“You think that makes it better?”

“No.”

He could have told her about the people who had been asking about him since the reception. About the copies of the footage he had not been able to have taken down. He had no right to give her more only when he wanted to keep her close. So he said nothing.

She unlocked the garage and pushed the side door open. “Go, Haozhen.”

He didn’t move. “Are you safe?”

Her face changed. Not softer. Worse. “Don’t ask me that.”

He swallowed. “All right.”

He walked away up the alley with his shoulders straight and his hands still in his pockets, and didn’t look back. At the corner he paused for one second.

Inside, the garage was cold. His mug was still upside down on the bench. She looked at it for a long time. Then she turned the lights on, and picked up her wrench, and went back to work, and for the first time she did not leave a space for him beside her.
